issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction may be restored in an appeal against acquittal when credible eyewitness testimony proves the accused inflicted the fatal injury and the reasons for rejecting that testimony are merely technical.
material_facts: A witness who was naturally present in the home testified that the accused fired at her husband, causing a fatal injury.

The witness’s account was challenged over her description of the firearms, the sequence of shots, and the injuries to another participant, but the Court found these discrepancies did not undermine the central account.
The medical evidence did not establish that the deceased was incapable of firing a weapon, and the Court found no fundamental conflict between that evidence and the eyewitness account.
The delayed transmission of the first information report and failures to seize firearms, spent cartridges, and bloodstained clothing did not displace the eyewitness testimony.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal on the murder charge concerning the deceased husband was set aside, and the trial court’s conviction was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, a credible eyewitness account may establish murder. Ocular testimony is ordinarily preferred over medical evidence unless it contradicts fundamental facts. A witness’s account must be assessed in the circumstances of the event and with due regard to a rural witness’s background; technical discrepancies and investigative omissions do not by themselves make reliable testimony unacceptable. The Court accepted that appellate restraint in appeals against acquittal is an established principle, citing State of Haryana v. Sher Singh, State of U.P. v. Ram Bahadur Singh, Chanakya Dhibar v. State of West Bengal, and Vijaybhai Bhanabhai Patel v. Navnitbhai Nathubhai Patel, but found that principle did not preclude correction of the High Court’s error on these facts.

rule.if: state_appeal_against_acquittal and eyewitness_directly_identifies_accused_as_fatal_shooter and eyewitness_account_is_credible and not fundamental_conflict_with_medical_evidence

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against an acquittal on the charge at issue.
predicates.eyewitness_directly_identifies_accused_a: An eyewitness testified that the accused fired the shot that caused the deceased’s fatal injury.
predicates.eyewitness_account_is_credible: The Court found the eyewitness’s account reliable despite challenges based on peripheral discrepancies or investigative omissions.
predicates.fundamental_conflict_with_medical_eviden: The medical evidence fundamentally contradicted the eyewitness’s account.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, a credible eyewitness account identifying the accused as the fatal shooter, without a fundamental medical contradiction, supports restoring the murder conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for criminal trespass with intent to commit an offence may be restored when credible testimony establishes that the accused entered a home to carry out a murderous assault.
material_facts: The eyewitness testified that the accused and other armed men entered the home.
She described the group’s entry and the ensuing armed assault on her husband.
The Court accepted her testimony as reliable.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal on the house-trespass charge was set aside, and the trial court’s conviction was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 449 of the Indian Penal Code applies where a person commits house-trespass in order to commit an offence punishable with death. The Court found the eyewitness’s testimony established entry into the home for the purpose of a murderous assault.

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against an acquittal on the charge at issue.
predicates.credible_witness_proves_entry_into_home: A witness whose testimony the Court accepted testified that the accused entered a home.
predicates.entry_was_for_murderous_assault: The evidence showed that the entry was made to carry out a murderous assault.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, credible proof that the accused entered a home to carry out a murderous assault supports restoring the trespass conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for attempted murder committed in furtherance of common intention may be restored when reliable evidence establishes the armed group’s attack and the resulting serious injury to a witness.
material_facts: An injured witness testified that an armed assailant fired at him and that a shot struck his arm.
The Court accepted that testimony as establishing the attack and found that it corroborated the account of the armed assault by the group.
The trial court had convicted the accused for the injury under Sections 307 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, and the High Court had acquitted him.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal on the charge concerning the shooting and injury of the witness was set aside, and the trial court’s conviction under Sections 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 307 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code provide for liability for an act done with the intention or knowledge required for attempted murder and for acts done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. The Court relied on the injured witness’s categorical testimony that an assailant fired at him and hit his arm, and held the charge established against the accused.

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against an acquittal on the charge at issue.
predicates.injured_witness_reliably_describes_armed: A witness injured in the incident reliably testified that an armed assailant fired at him and caused an injury.
predicates.accused_participated_in_attack_in_furthe: The evidence established that the accused participated in the group attack carried out in furtherance of a shared intention.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, reliable testimony about an armed group attack causing injury, together with proof of the accused’s participation in furtherance of common intention, supports restoring the attempted-murder conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for murder with the aid of common intention cannot be sustained when the evidence does not reliably establish the accused’s responsibility for the death.
material_facts: The charge concerned the death of a person other than the deceased whose shooting was described by the principal eyewitness.
The witness relied on to connect the accused to that death claimed to have watched events through an iron grill, but the Court found there was no such grill at the asserted vantage point.
Another witness’s account was not convincing because he observed the incident from a considerable distance.
The Court found the evidence insufficient to uphold the charge against the accused.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal on the charge of murder with common intention concerning the other deceased was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code require proof of murder and, for joint liability, that the act was done in furtherance of a common intention. The Court found that the asserted eyewitness vantage point was unsupported and the other account was unconvincing, leaving insufficient evidence to sustain the charge.

predicates.state_appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against an acquittal on the charge at issue.
predicates.claimed_eyewitness_vantage_is_impossible: The physical features of the claimed observation point did not allow the witness to see the incident as described.
predicates.other_account_does_not_reliably_identify: The remaining witness’s account was not convincing enough to establish the accused’s responsibility for the death.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, an impossible claimed vantage point and an unconvincing remaining account leave the acquittal in place.
